w06.001: Conclusions: The Purpose of the Master Universe and the Seven Questions
w06.003: Having finished the body of his study, Sadler returns to the questions he posed in the Introduction and takes stock. The master universe cannot be described by size and duration alone. Seen from the creature's side, it is a larger home in which we are born, grow up, and prepare for the Absolute Adventure; seen from the side of Deity, it is the ground from which two experiential Deities and two experiential Trinities arise. Sadler answers his seven questions one by one and then gathers the nine themes, principles, and patterns that kept reappearing throughout the work.
w06.004: 1. Looking Back on a Long Journey (orig. p. 116)
w06.005: Sadler's study set out from the dawn of time, the opening of the second universe age. "The Finite Story" began when Havona stood before the imperfect superuniverses as the thesis of perfection, and it closed once the superuniverses were finished and the Supreme Being had emerged. "The Subabsolute Story" then began when the grand universe stood as a second thesis before the creations of outer space, and it ran on until God the Ultimate appeared and the vast master universe was complete.
w06.006: The cycle of thesis, antithesis, and synthesis has thus run its full course twice. A third cycle has been seen only at its beginning, not at its end. At this point, Sadler says, the main body of the study has reached its logical close. The epilogue that follows is a separate venture, one that stands outside the main argument and looks beyond the master universe.
w06.007: 2. What Is the Master Universe For? (orig. pp. 116–117)
w06.009: At the very start of the Introduction Sadler asked what the master universe really is, how the purposes of God unfold within it, and what purpose the master universe itself serves (Chapter 4). In the Conclusions he judges his own work candidly. He has learned something about physical dimensions and about the length of the universe ages, but on the purposes of God and of the master universe he may have done little more than scratch the surface.
w06.010: Even so, he offers one conclusion. The master universe is the stage for God's adventure into relative reality, that is, into the finite and absonite realities that lie below the absolute level. Part of that adventure is to discover whether the loyalty of creatures like ourselves can be won by nothing other than the persuasive power of love.
w06.011: Here Sadler adds a word about the attitude of faith. Schemes for bargaining with God over survival, whether by good works or by a carefully calculated ethics, are of little worth. What matters instead is the response to the challenge of love, the invitation to share in divine perfection. That response leads first into the near-term adventure of ascending to Paradise and, further on, into the everlasting adventure of exploring how infinite God is and how infinite His love is.
w06.012: The Master Universe as Creatures See It
w06.013: For the creature the master universe is a "larger home." There we are born and grow, make our decisions, ascend in search of God, fulfill our finite destiny, and then go on to growth on absonite levels. In Sadler's view we come of age only after our absonite destiny has also been filled out. At that point, as seasoned citizens of the master creation, we will be qualified to set out on the last experiential adventure: the eternal search for the Father as the Absolute. Seen this way, the entire master universe career is a preparation for the final challenge Sadler names the Absolute Adventure. The master universe is a nursery in which the children of experience are raised, and one day they will take part in building the endless Cosmos Infinite.
w06.014: The Master Universe as Deity Sees It
w06.015: From the standpoint of Deity, Sadler sums up the purposes of the master universe under four heads. Two concern Deity: how the Supreme Being evolves and emerges, and how God the Ultimate does likewise. Two concern Trinity: the forming of the Trinity Ultimate and of the Trinity Absolute. These four are linked like a chain. No experiential Trinity can exist without experiential Deity, and unless both experiential Trinities exist, the Trinity of Trinities cannot be woven together.

w06.016.q: 2. The Absolute Trinity—the second experiential Trinity—now in process of actualization, will consist of God the Supreme, God the Ultimate, and the unrevealed Consummator of Universe Destiny.

w06.017: At the far end of this chain Sadler sees total actualized Deity reunited in the existential-experiential Trinity of Trinities. In his reading, God, who in the eternal past expressed Himself existentially in Paradise and Havona, intends in the eternal future to express Himself experientially, using the master universe as His platform.
w06.018: 3. Answers to the Seven Questions (orig. pp. 118–119)
w06.019: At the end of the Introduction Sadler posed seven questions (Chapter 4). Now he goes through them like items on a checklist. His answers can be summarized as follows.
w06.020: The seven questions of the Introduction and Sadler's answers in the Conclusions
w06.022: (1) How large are the space levels?
Their sizes differ greatly. The grand universe is small next to the outer universes, and the levels grow sharply larger out to the Quartan Space Level.
w06.023: (2) How long are the universe ages?
The second age lasts roughly 50,000 times as long as our sun's parent nebula has existed (about one trillion years), and the ages of outer space are far longer. The ages also differ in kind.
w06.024: (3) How are the experiential Deities and Trinities related to the space levels and ages?
Through the relation of nuclear universe to cytoplasmic universe. Each new Deity and new Trinity appears together with a nuclear universe.
w06.025: (4) What themes, patterns, and principles can be found?
Nine of them (Section 4 of this chapter).
w06.026: Finaliters go on growing through the supreme, the post-supreme, and the post-ultimate levels, and they never run into a final limit of growth.
w06.027: (6) Is the master universe the last creation?
No. It is the third (and perhaps last) nuclear universe, and a still larger cytoplasmic creation must lie beyond it.
w06.028: (7) What are the final limit and the final goal?
This cannot be answered within a study of the master universe, except that both lie outside it.
w06.030: In answering the second question, Sadler stresses character more than length. The first age is unique because it is the age of past eternity. The second age is likewise unique, being the age in which the Supreme Being grows. The four ages of outer space resemble one another and can be treated as a group: they follow the completion of the Supreme's growth, and they are the ages in which God the Ultimate grows. Beyond them Sadler anticipates a post-ultimate "Final Age," an age of future eternity that has a beginning but no end.
w06.032: The answer to the third question exposes the skeleton of the whole study. Not all universes are alike. Some are nuclei, and others are the cytoplasm that depends on those nuclei. Sadler identified three nuclear universes appearing one after another: Havona serves as nucleus to the superuniverses, the grand universe serves as nucleus to the outer universes, and the master universe serves as nucleus to the Cosmos Infinite.
w06.033: The threefold nucleus: each nuclear universe is paired with a new Deity and a new Trinity (the Cosmos Infinite is Sadler's concept)
w06.034: A new Deity and a new Trinity always appear along with a nuclear universe. The existential central creation is paired with existential Deity and the Paradise Trinity; the experiential grand universe and master universe are paired with experiential Deities and experiential Trinities. Just as the nucleus of a cell directs the life of the whole cytoplasm, a nuclear universe functions on behalf of the creation that grows around it and depends on it.
w06.036: The answer to the fifth question comes closest to human concerns. According to Sadler, finaliters possess the personality and the endowment to keep on with every kind of post-Havona growth to the very end. They grow forever and yet meet no absolute barrier. If their goals widen faster than they themselves grow, they will never actually reach an infinite goal; yet in that endless advance they are never blocked or thwarted. A traveler walking toward the horizon never arrives at it, but the road itself never runs out.
w06.037: 4. Nine Themes, Principles, and Patterns (orig. pp. 120–122)
w06.038: The seventh question went unanswered, but Sadler says he found a good deal in reply to the fourth. He names nine themes that, in his view, thread their way through the whole creative plan of the master universe.
w06.039: The nine themes, principles, and patterns identified by Sadler
w06.041: An original thesis is confronted by a stimulating antithesis; the two are unified and enlarged together.
w06.042: A great synthesis shows itself in the emergence of a new Deity; that Deity gives rise to a new Trinity, and the Trinity becomes a new thesis.
w06.043: Havona, the grand universe, and the master universe become nuclei in turn.
w06.044: IV Cytoplasmic need enlarges nuclear function
The deficiency of the outer creation calls the nuclear universe to service, and in responding the nucleus outgrows its earlier limits.
w06.045: Experiential growth, on the level of Deity and of the creature alike, is a union of power and personality.
w06.046: VI Creative partnership of dual Deity
Dual Deity works on the frontiers of creation; the Trinity governs the finished universe.
w06.047: Reality branches into diversity to avoid monotony and is brought together again in experiential Deity.
w06.048: Like a living organism, the universe is consistent in its acts and their outcomes. Omnipotence does not mean doing the impossible.
w06.049: IX Trinitization as escape from infinity
As God "escaped" the limits of infinity through trinitization, the experiential Deities seek to "enter" infinity.
w06.051: The fourth principle sets the third in motion. A cytoplasmic creation begins by lacking something that the nuclear universe had (or has). The superuniverses lack the perfection of Havona; the outer universes, it seems, will be without finite experience. This lack becomes a challenge to the nuclear creation, which grows as it answers with service. In the present age Havona is adding evolutionary growth to its eternal perfection (Chapter 5). In the next age the superuniverses, settled in light and life, will add growth possibilities not yet known on top of their present evolutionary limits. Sadler goes a step further and guesses that what the Cosmos Infinite may give the master universe is the opening of growth on a "co-absolute" level for creatures who have exhausted every finite and absonite possibility.
w06.053: The fifth principle threads Deity and humanity on one string. For a human being, the union of power and personality comes about when mind, which governs matter, places itself under the leading of spirit by the free choice of the personality. On the level of Deity it means that all the things, meanings, and values of a given level, that is, all its material, mental, and spiritual reality, are gathered and consolidated in an experiential Deity: the finite in the Supreme Being, the absonite in God the Ultimate (Chapters 7 and 13).
w06.054: In the sixth principle Sadler observes how the partnerships of dual Deity shift from age to age. In the first age the Father-Son, in the second the Son-Spirit, and in the ages of outer space the Spirit-Supreme take the lead in pioneering. The chain continues to the Supreme-Ultimate and beyond, but inside the master universe it can be followed only as far as the Spirit-Supreme. That restriction is lifted again in the epilogue.
w06.055: The seventh principle is illustrated by the Seven Master Spirits. They express the unity of Paradise Deity in seven different ways, and that diversity is reunited finitely in the Supreme and absonitely in the Ultimate. Each superuniverse develops a distinctive culture reflecting the nature of its supervising Master Spirit, and after the Supreme Being has fully emerged the seven cultures will merge into one. Sadler compares this to the way the races of an evolutionary world each build their own culture and then blend within the Adamic civilization.
w06.057: If the superuniverses have seven cultures, Sadler suggests, there may be forty-nine on the Primary Space Level and still more on the levels beyond. That each of the seven superuniverses is under one of the Seven Master Spirits is the teaching of The Urantia Book. The idea that diversity in outer space multiplies by powers of seven, however, is Sadler's conjecture, an extension of the pattern of divergence and convergence. No such figure appears in the text.
w06.059: Sadler himself admits that the ninth principle was not, strictly speaking, learned from the study of the master universe. It is a pre-master-universe principle, and perhaps a post-master-universe one as well. In the prologue God freed Himself from the limitations inherent in the state of infinity by means of trinitization (Chapter 1). At the end of the main study the inquiry ran up against the Barrier of Infinity and then the Impasse of the Absolutes, and the effort to unify the second experiential Trinity came to a standstill (Chapter 16). Sadler announces that in the epilogue a similar situation will be met again, but with the direction reversed. God came out of infinity; the experiential Deities seek to go into it.
w06.060: Sadler's main study completes two cycles of thesis, antithesis, and synthesis and stops at the threshold of the third. The epilogue is a separate attempt to look beyond the master universe.
w06.061: Sadler regards the master universe as the stage for God's adventure into relative reality. Part of that adventure is to win the loyalty of creatures by love alone.
w06.062: For creatures the master universe is a "larger home" and a school of preparation for the Absolute Adventure; for Deity it is the ground from which two experiential Deities and two experiential Trinities arise.
w06.063: Six of the seven questions receive answers; of the final limit and the final goal, Sadler can confirm only that they lie outside the master universe.
w06.064: Havona, the grand universe, and the master universe become nuclear universes in turn, and each nuclear universe is always paired with a new Deity and a new Trinity.
w06.065: The need of a cytoplasmic creation calls the nuclear creation to service, and in responding the nucleus passes beyond its former limits of growth.
w06.066: The ninth principle, trinitization, is the key to the epilogue: God came out of infinity, and the experiential Deities seek to enter it.
w06.067: The Epilogue in Eternity and the Afterword
w06.068: Epilogue in Eternity (First to Third) · Afterword (pp. 123–146)
w06.069: Where the prologue dealt with what existential Deity did before creation, the epilogue imagines what experiential Deity may do beyond creation. Distinguishing quality from quantity, Sadler pictures God the Supreme and God the Ultimate together trinitizing God the Absolute, with the Cosmos Infinite opening at the same time. He then looks ahead to the three phases of the Final Age, the last partnerships of dual Deity, and the last three levels on which total Deity functions, and he closes, as he began, with the Infinite. In the Afterword Sadler calls The Urantia Book a story of love and adventure and names God as its true hero.
w06.070: 1. A New Start from the Impasse (orig. pp. 123–124)
w06.071: An Epilogue to Match the Prologue
w06.072: The "Prologue in Eternity" at the head of the study examined what existential Deity did before creation. Those acts set the stage for the whole story, in which Paradise creativity surges outward and its results are gathered again on supreme and ultimate levels. Now, at the opposite end, the epilogue tries to picture what experiential Deity might do beyond creation: acts that pierce the Barrier of Infinity and, to some degree, get around the Impasse of the Absolutes. The epilogue has three parts. The first treats the Final Age, the second the depths of that age, and the third what comes after "the end of the end."
w06.074: Sadler acknowledges that the main study ended on a clear note of frustration. The unstoppable force of the Trinity Absolute met the immovable fact of eternal infinity and came to an impasse. The unification of the Trinity Absolute is a task without end, and so the Trinity of Trinities is also incomplete. On its first level one member, the Trinity Absolute, is not unified; on its second level one member, God the Absolute, is missing altogether.
w06.075: Moreover, the master universe, now mobilized as a nuclear universe, as yet has no cytoplasm around it. The space surrounding it is still empty. Every nebula of the master universe was organized by force organizers, who act for the Master Architects, and Sadler doubts that the Architects' plans reach beyond the borders of the master creation. Where, then, is the way out?
w06.077: The clue Sadler finds is the distinction between quality and quantity. He proposes to pair the word "absolute" with undiminished quality and the word "infinite" with unlimited quantity. Once the two are separated, absolute destiny can be reached in a way that is not infinite: limited in quantity, perhaps, yet complete in quality.
w06.078: His illustration is a homely one. No one can breathe in all the air of the earth in a lifetime. Yet that limit of quantity does not mean one cannot breathe at all, nor does it lower the quality of the air one takes in. The air in a single breath is air in the full sense.
w06.079: Havona is the example. At the trinitization of the Spirit by the Father and the Son, when Havona came into being, the Deities poured the full quality of divine perfection into that central creation, holding nothing back. Its quantity, however, they did not make infinite; otherwise all of eternal space would have been occupied by one existentially perfect universe. The Deities kept Havona to one billion worlds and a bounded space. They did not bring the master universe into being existentially, nor did they eternalize the Cosmos Infinite by a single command. Because quantity was limited in this way, all the experiential development after Havona became possible. In the same manner, Sadler concludes, by limiting how much absoluteness could be experientialized, the Deities prepared the path of endless growth.
w06.080: The Urantia Book also thinks in terms of quality and quantity, in a passage that discusses the total function of the Trinity Absolute.

w06.081.q: And it would also appear that the unconditioned would also be unlimited, at least from a qualitative standpoint, though we are not so sure regarding quantitative relationships.

w06.082: Sadler points out that the only alternative to endless growth is growth that ends. And what would follow then? A universe whose growth has ended is a universe with nowhere left to go.
w06.083: 3. The Trinitization That Opens the Final Age (orig. pp. 125–127)
w06.084: The Symmetry of the First Age and the Final Age
w06.085: Sadler proposes to examine the Final Age with the same care he gave the first age in the third prologue. The two ages are symmetrical. The first age has an end yet never began in time; the Final Age begins in time yet never ends. One is a reality of past eternity, the other a reality of future eternity.
w06.086: An inventory of what was actual when the first age dawned lists a pair of existential Deities, Father and Son, together with a base of operations, the Isle of Paradise. Joined as the Father-Son, the Father and the Son trinitized the Infinite Spirit, a coordinate Deity; as a result Havona appeared and the Paradise Trinity was formed (Chapters 1 and 3).
w06.087: Sadler expects a similar inventory when the Final Age dawns: a pair of experiential Deities, Supreme and Ultimate, together with a base of operations, the finished master universe. He believes universe history will repeat itself. The Supreme and the Ultimate, joined as the Supreme-Ultimate, will trinitize God the Absolute, a coordinate Deity; as a result the Cosmos Infinite will begin and the Trinity of Trinities will be woven together. What took place existentially in the first age would thus be repeated experientially in the Final Age.
w06.088: Trinitization in the first age and in the Final Age: the existential original and its experiential repetition (the right-hand column is Sadler's inference)
w06.089: There are differences as well. Because the Father and the Son are both existential and infinite, whatever they bring forth is existential and infinite too. The Supreme and the Ultimate are experiential Deities, less than infinite, so God the Absolute, their product, would likewise be an experiential and qualified expression. Yet both are almighty, and so they can mobilize the entire actualized experiential reality contained in the completed master universe. In Chapter 12 Sadler likened the grand universe to a tennis ball and the master universe to a large moon; everything "from the tennis ball to the moon" would be brought to bear on this act. The first trinitization was precreative, the last one supercreative. Since the ultimate level is the last creative level, Sadler explains, the Supreme-Ultimate and God the Absolute, who appear after it, are supercreative manifestations.
w06.090: Two Brothers with a Battering Ram
w06.091: Sadler holds the scene in his mind as a single picture. Two experiential brothers, an elder and a younger, shoulder an enormous battering ram and take their stand before a wall inscribed "Infinity." Loaded into the ram is all the power gained in achieving experiential sovereignty over the entire master universe. The elder brother urges the younger to swing with all his might, for they mean to break in. Both are well aware that the wall itself cannot be demolished. But they also know they can breach it, and that they will. What gives the ram its weight is every experiential thing, meaning, and value in the universe, mobilized as power-personality.
w06.092: 4. A New Transformation of Synthesis (orig. pp. 127–128)
w06.094: In Chapter 9 Sadler traced how a former synthesis turns into a fresh thesis. When the finite was completed, the synthesis in the Supreme Being gave rise to a new thesis, the first experiential Trinity; when the absonite was completed, the synthesis in God the Ultimate gave rise to a new thesis, the second experiential Trinity. The Supreme and the Ultimate were, respectively, "the synthesis of the total finite" and "the synthesis of the total absonite."
w06.095: Now Sadler sees a new kind of transformation. In their trinitizing union the two experiential Deities themselves become new theses. The Supreme becomes the thesis of the total finite, the Ultimate the thesis of the total absonite, and God the Absolute, whom they trinitize, becomes a third thesis, the experiential thesis of the (qualified) absolute. Thesis is laid upon thesis.
w06.096: Has anything like this happened before? Sadler answers that something similar appeared in the prologue. In coming out of infinity, God established the Son as the absolute thesis of Deity, and, as the Father of the Son, established Himself as the prethesis of Deity. The Father-Son in turn established the Spirit as the associative thesis of Deity. This threefold layering culminates in the Paradise Trinity, the thesis of undivided existential Deity. In the same way, Sadler holds, the threefold thesis of experiential Deity (Supreme, Ultimate, and Absolute) finds qualitative unity on the Trinity of Trinities' second level, and in that process it expands outward as the undivided thesis of total Deity, at once existential and experiential.
w06.098: Sadler insists repeatedly that the parallel is analogous, not homologous. In trinitizing the Spirit, the Father-Son was emerging from infinity; in trinitizing God the Absolute, the Supreme-Ultimate seeks to enter infinity. What the Father-Son achieved in both quality and quantity, the Supreme-Ultimate can achieve only in quality. God the Absolute appears as absolute reality in quality, but in quantity and universality He is the manifestation of an Absolute that is less than infinite.
w06.099: 5. The Cosmos Infinite Begins; the Trinity of Trinities Takes Shape (orig. pp. 128–130)
w06.100: The First Installment of the Cosmos Infinite
w06.101: Sadler regards the trinitized appearance of God the Absolute as the most profound event in universe history since the appearance of the Infinite Spirit. Just as the Infinite Spirit became personal together with the appearance of an eternal universe (Havona), so the appearance of God the Absolute will be accompanied by the beginning of the Cosmos Infinite. The first creation is actually eternal; the last creation is potentially infinite. Since the Supreme and the Ultimate can mobilize physical as well as spiritual potentials, their union is total and leaves nothing out. Sadler therefore infers that God the Absolute will appear at the same moment that the innermost zone of the Cosmos Infinite is materialized.
w06.102: What will this "first installment" of the Cosmos Infinite be like? As he said in Chapter 15, Sadler thinks it will be unlike anything that has appeared in the master creation. For the first time even the transcendental designs of the Master Architects will themselves be surpassed. He adds, however, that certain existential aspects of eternal Havona might give a hint of the character of this new domain.
w06.103: About its size we can only guess. With the grand universe set at the size of a tennis ball, the master universe was a moon 3,200 miles across. Sadler expects the same ratio to repeat once more. Shrink the master universe to a tennis ball, and the Cosmos Infinite's innermost zone would match the moon in size. And that is only the innermost zone, probably the smallest. His grounds are the earlier cases. Havona is very small compared with the size (though not the mass) of the superuniverses, and the grand universe is small compared with the master universe. A nucleus has always been small next to the cytoplasm it governs.
w06.105: The appearance of God the Absolute offers one more parallel to the appearance of the Infinite Spirit: both lead to the formation of a Trinity. As the Infinite Spirit completed the personalization of existential Deity and so made the Paradise Trinity possible, the (qualified) appearance of God the Absolute would in effect complete the second level of the Trinity of Trinities. The Urantia Book says that various theories are held about the third member of this second level.

w06.106.q: God the Absolute is undoubtedly involved in this association as the personality consequence of the final function of the Trinity Absolute, yet the Deity Absolute is an existential reality of eternity status.

w06.107: About the third level even Sadler is not certain. As long as God the Absolute remains forever incomplete in the quantitative sense, he thinks, the third level will be occupied by the Universal Absolute. This judgment rests on the following words of the text.

w06.108.q: It will probably represent a minimum distortion of truth if the third member of the Trinity of Trinities is conceived as the Universal Absolute…

w06.109: The Trinity of Trinities as Sadler pictures it after the appearance of God the Absolute
w06.110: Should God the Absolute ever finish His experiential growth, we would find ourselves outside infinity, beyond the end of eternity. What Sadler means is that this will never happen.
w06.111: 6. The Depths of the Final Age: Three Phases and the Third Experiential Trinity (orig. pp. 131–134)
w06.113: Once the Barrier of Infinity is breached, the whole of future eternity lies open to endless speculation. To keep thought from being swept away on a sea of "what ifs" into absurdity, Sadler proposes to build levees around it. He divides the development of the Cosmos Infinite into three phases. Phase One is the innermost zone, made factual together with the appearance of God the Absolute, and it is matched with the Supreme-Ultimate. Phase Two is the intermediate stage of development that follows; it may or may not have an end, and it is matched with the Ultimate-Absolute. Phase Three may be a purely theoretical final stage, matched with the association of the Absolute and the Father-Infinite, the "completion" of the cycle of reality.
w06.114: The reason for three divisions is simple. To hold the ideas of beginning, middle, and destiny, or of inception, realization, and consummation, at least three compartments are needed. In practice there might as well be seven, or a million. The triad of inception, realization, and consummation comes from the language The Urantia Book uses in describing the Trinity of Trinities [106:8.12].
w06.116: Sadler puts forward the proposition that the second level of the Trinity of Trinities is itself another trinity, the "Third Experiential Trinity." His ground is the likeness of origins. At the start, Father and Son, united as the Father-Son, trinitized the Spirit, who completes existential Deity as its third person, and these three became the Paradise Trinity. In the end the Supreme and the Ultimate, united as the Supreme-Ultimate, trinitize God the Absolute, who becomes experiential Deity's third person, and these three become the final experiential Trinity.
w06.117: One difference is decisive. The Spirit "completes" the actualization of existential Deity, whereas God the Absolute "begins" the final actualization of experiential Deity. The trinitization by the Father-Son was an act of unbounded infinity; the trinitization by the Supreme-Ultimate is absolute in quality but not infinite in quantity. The Infinite Spirit, eternalized as a completed being, has little room to grow; God the Absolute, in whom only a portion of the Deity Absolute's infinity has become actual, stands at the threshold of limitless growth. The difference between the potentially infinite and the actually infinite is the difference between growth and nongrowth.
w06.118: Sadler concludes that this Third Experiential Trinity differs from every other trinity. It is the only one composed solely of experiential Deities. Like the Paradise Trinity, it has a trinitized third member, yet it differs in that it is still growing, expanding, and being unified. It is also the only trinity contained within another trinity, the Trinity of Trinities.
w06.119: The Growth of God the Absolute
w06.120: Sadler foresees three relationships in which God the Absolute will grow. The first is with the Trinity Absolute, which is not yet unified. Ordinarily that Trinity would have to be unified before God the Absolute could appear; having appeared first by the method of trinitization, God the Absolute now cooperates with His "ancestral" Trinity. The second is with the Supreme-Ultimate. As the Spirit expresses the Father-Son partnership intensively, God the Absolute expresses the Supreme-Ultimate partnership extensively and grows along with it. The third, and most distinctive, is with the Deity Absolute. Because God the Absolute has been actualized from only part of the infinite potential of the Deity Absolute, an untouched infinity of potential remains outside Him. He expands outward into that potential, and this expansion is His growth. Since the room for growth is infinite, the growth never ends.
w06.122: The Urantia Book speaks of God the Absolute as "⟦Q 106:8.16⟧the personality consequence of the final function of the Trinity Absolute⟦/Q⟧" [106:8.16]. Taken in order, the Trinity Absolute would first be unified, and God the Absolute would then appear as its result. Sadler is aware of this order, and so he offers the interpretation that God the Absolute appears "ahead of time" by the different route of trinitization and then cooperates with the still-ununified Trinity Absolute. This is Sadler's own construction, an attempt to fill a gap the text leaves open. Also, where the original (p. 134) describes the Trinity of Trinities as "existential-existential," this appears to be a slip for "existential-experiential" [cf. 0:12.9].
w06.123: 7. The Last Partnerships of Dual Deity (orig. pp. 135–139)
w06.124: Dual Deity Pioneers, the Trinity Consolidates
w06.125: Throughout the study Sadler has watched one principle at work: dual Deity pioneers, and the Trinity consolidates. Will the principle still hold beyond the master universe? He brings back the six partnerships that The Urantia Book makes known.

w06.126.q: The Father-Son partnership has become Son-Spirit and then Spirit-Supreme and on to Supreme-Ultimate and Ultimate-Absolute, even to Absolute and Father-Infinite—the completion of the cycle of reality.

w06.127: Sadler sorts these six into four categories: eternity (Father-Son), the master universe (Son-Spirit and Spirit-Supreme), post-master-universe (Supreme-Ultimate and Ultimate-Absolute), and future eternity (Absolute and Father-Infinite). These associations begin as existential, become progressively more experiential, and at last move in an experiential-existential direction.
w06.128: The six partnerships of dual Deity and "The Processional of Initiative" (the grouping and the matching with phases are Sadler's interpretation)
w06.130: Sadler gives this sequence the name "The Processional of Initiative." The idea is that God hands a share of the initiative in creative self-expression to His coordinates, and wants that share to be as full as they can bear. God opens reality when He becomes Father to the Original Son, and with that Son He makes the Creator Sons. The Creator Sons enjoy full sonship toward the Paradise Deities, yet in their own evolving universes they become experiential fathers. In the Father-Son relationship the Spirit was personalized as the coordinate agency that gives expression to Havona; in the Son-Spirit relationship the Spirit, through the Creative Spirits, becomes the "second creator" of the local universes. What the Eternal Son "experienced" on Paradise in eternity, the Spirit's spirits experience in time and space. In the third phase, the Spirit-Supreme, Sadler expects the Spirit to take new initiative in outer space, assisted by the Supreme Being, whose growth is by then complete. Because the text says nothing of the outcome, he does not speculate about it.
w06.132: The last three partnerships lie beyond the master universe, since they involve the Ultimate, who effectively comes on stage only after the entire master creation is finished. Sadler compares the Supreme-Ultimate to the Father-Son. Each trinitizes the third person of a Deity, each opens a universe (the universe of eternity and the universe of infinity), and each forms a trinity together with that third person. But whereas the Father-Son initiates, realizes, and consummates, the Supreme-Ultimate initiates and partly realizes, and does not consummate.
w06.133: Phase One, opened by the Supreme-Ultimate, will be immensely long. Sadler says that thinking about it is like asking a machinist who works in ten-thousandths of an inch to picture the size of a galaxy millions of light-years away. With the Ultimate-Absolute, speculation grows harder still, and he proceeds by analogy. As the Son-Spirit grew out of the Father-Son, the Ultimate-Absolute will grow out of the Supreme-Ultimate and take charge of the intermediate phase of the Cosmos Infinite, its "realization." Yet this partnership can hardly attain even a qualitative destiny; it can begin but can never be finished. Even if the innermost zone appears suddenly, as Havona did, the growth that follows, if sequential, has no end.
w06.134: Sadler inserts a parenthesis here. The Ultimate-Absolute is not only a matter of the remote future; even now, in the grand universe, it is real as a level of value. The text describes the destiny of Personalized Adjusters this way.

w06.135.q: …and they are thus both destined to the future eternal superpersonality of the transcendental ministry of the absonite realms of the Ultimate, the Supreme-Ultimate, even to the levels of the Ultimate-Absolute.

w06.136: A Personalized Adjuster is the very fragment of God that fuses with us, now personalized. If such Adjusters can serve as high as the Ultimate-Absolute level, Sadler reasons, finaliters too will function there, given enough time and growth.
w06.138: The final partnership, the Absolute and the Father-Infinite, is the "completion" of the cycle of reality. Sadler sees it as an existential-experiential association. Existentially it is always present; experientially it is always distant; existential-experientially it is a "becoming reality." However far actualization advances, the potential that will never be expressed is not reduced in the least. If this is a relationship of pure eternity, it becomes meaningless to speak of growth by comparison with past or future. As Sadler puts it, the relationship may not lie beyond concept, but it surely lies beyond comprehensible concept.
w06.139: 8. The Last Three Levels of Total Deity Function (orig. pp. 139–142)
w06.141: The Urantia Book says that total Deity functions on seven levels [0:1.3]. In the second prologue Sadler examined the static, potential, and associative levels, and in the main study the outward-reaching creative and evolutional levels and the inward-reaching supreme and ultimate levels. Yet the ultimate level is the last creative level, and God the Absolute is supercreative. None of the seven levels is called an absolute level; the absolute level is mentioned as the level the Paradise Trinity has attained existentially.

w06.142.q: This level is Trinity attained, existentially, by the Paradise Deities, but this third level of unifying Deity expression is not fully unified experientially.

w06.143: Sadler believes that until the experiential Deities are factualized these seven levels are all there are, but that once the three experiential Deities are factualized, three more levels of total Deity function will come to light. Existential Deity arises within infinity and moves outward from it; experiential Deity arises outside infinity and strives to break into it. Were existential Deity to return to infinity, it would retrace its course from the associative level to the potential and then back to the static. The approach of experiential Deity is different. The three levels Sadler names are the Reassociative Level, the Actualizing-Potential Level, and the Static-Dynamic Level.
w06.144: The ten levels of total Deity function: the last three mirror the first three (levels 8–10 are Sadler's concepts)
w06.146: The last three levels are mirror images of the first three. The reassociative (8) answers to the associative (3); the actualizing-potential (9) answers to the potential (2); and the static-dynamic (10) answers to the static (1). Sadler explains that destiny mirrors source: absolute values stay the same, and only meanings change. The value of the infinite does not alter, but the relationships of the infinite, which are its meanings, can change almost without limit.
w06.147: The best example of the reassociative level is the Trinity of Trinities. If the associative level is represented by the Paradise Trinity, which unifies existential Deity absolutely, then on the reassociative level every actualization of Deity, existential or experiential, is gathered together again. Experientially the Trinity of Trinities is always incomplete, but since its member the Paradise Trinity is existentially infinite, that incompleteness can always be made good.

w06.148.q: But irrespective of all this, the original Paradise Trinity is potentially infinite since the Universal Father actually is infinite.

w06.149: For the actualizing-potential level Sadler chooses the name with care. To speak of "actualized potential" would imply that the potential has been used up; since potential has no end, the progressive form "actualizing" is the right one. Full quantitative attainment of this level would require three things: the Unqualified Absolute's capacity used up entirely, so that the Cosmos Infinite became an actual universe without outside or end; the Deity Absolute's capacity likewise used up, so that God the Absolute was completed as an experiential-absolute person of Deity coordinate with the Eternal Son; and the two perfectly synthesized as power-personality. That would amount to achieving experientially what the Universal Absolute does existentially.

w06.150.q: The improbability of infinite destiny attainment does not in the least prevent the entertainment of ideas about such destiny…

w06.151: Sadler says there is no need to be discouraged that this level can never be reached quantitatively. If all potential were actualized, all growth, all change, and all adventure would come to an end: an eternal today with no tomorrow. God in His wisdom has avoided this. His plan provides a universe forever young and growing, a creation always on the threshold of new adventure, a universe living perpetually in the dawn of an unending spring.
w06.153: The last level is the final reach of experiential Deity, and perhaps of experiential creatures, toward the Father as the Infinite. At the outset Sadler imagined God as the Infinite in "the static moment of eternity" at the center of the Zero Age (Chapter 2).

w06.154.q: Infinity is filled by the Infinite; the Infinite encompasses infinity. This is the hypothetical static moment of eternity…

w06.155: Now, as its counterpart, he imagines a "hypothetical static-dynamic moment of eternity" that exists in theory in the eternal future. If that moment could be reached, we would know the Father as the Infinite. Since it cannot, we will find the Father as the Absolute but go on forever seeking Him as the Infinite. Sadler understands the "shadow of infinity" that falls across the limitlessness of potential reality as the presence of the Universal Absolute. That mystery grows with the growing universe, and it may deepen faster than the finaliters themselves grow.
w06.156: 9. After the End of the End: Closing with the Infinite (orig. pp. 143–144)
w06.158: The third epilogue is brief. Sadler borrows The Urantia Book's image of all reality as a vast ellipse.

w06.159.q: The human mind, as it seeks to penetrate the eternity-mystery of the origin and destiny of all that is called real, may helpfully approach the problem by conceiving eternity-infinity as an almost limitless ellipse which is produced by one absolute cause, and which functions throughout this universal circle of endless diversification, ever seeking some absolute and infinite potential of destiny.

w06.160: What the first prologue called "source" the last epilogue calls "destiny," but at the beginning and at the end the object of the search is the same Source-Destiny: the Infinite, best known to us as God. Just as God bestowed His absolute nature on His firstborn Son and shared sovereignty over all creation in the Spirit and as the Trinity, so He is engaged in the eternal work of revealing Himself and sharing His nature with all His sons and the sons of His sons.
w06.162: However far the forces and personalities of creation spread, from Paradise to the depths of the Cosmos Infinite, the value of God neither increases nor decreases. The Infinite does not change. But for every being who takes part in the adventure, the meaning of God is altered, enriched, and enlarged.

w06.163.q: We do not comprehend how the value of anything infinite and divine could possibly be increased. But we discover that meanings can be modified if not augmented even in the relations of infinite Deity.

w06.165: Sadler sums up the future of the ascender as three adventures. In the Supreme Adventure we reach Paradise and find God, experience the whole of finite Deity by finding the Supreme at the close of the second age, and come to understand the Father as finite creatures can know Him, the Father as the Finite. The Ultimate Adventure is the search for the superfinite Father, the Father as the Absonite. It takes an extremely long time, but because it has a distant limit, we will one day actually come to know the Ultimate. The last, the Absolute Adventure, has no end. We will truly find God as the Absolute, yet we will never complete that finding, for the exploration of God's infinity must be endless.

w06.166.q: Sooner or later all universe personalities begin to realize that the final quest of eternity is the endless exploration of infinity, the never-ending voyage of discovery into the absoluteness of the First Source and Center.

w06.167: Still, we know the Infinite exists and is real, preceding the First Source and following the final destiny. The passage Sadler cites tells what kind of knowledge this is.

w06.168.q: God, your Father and my Father, is that phase of the Infinite which we perceive in our personalities as an actual experiential reality, but the I AM ever remains as our hypothesis of all that we feel is unknowable of the First Source and Center.

w06.169: Sadler closes the epilogue with the thought that even at the end of time the words of Hebrews 11:1, "faith is the substance of things hoped for," will still hold true.
w06.170: 10. Afterword: A Story of Love and Adventure (orig. pp. 145–146)
w06.171: In his Foreword Sadler likened The Urantia Book to a symphony (Chapter 1). In the Afterword he compares the same book to a romance, a tale of love and of adventure. What held him throughout his study was, on the one hand, divine love and, on the other, a spirit of adventure that seems to lie at the root of God's purposes.
w06.172: The God Sadler portrays gives without stint yet is never indulgent. The One who gives so much in love also sets challenges before those He loves. God is a maker of problems, and in solving them His children grow. While remaining changeless Himself, God is ever the cause of change. He places a new and challenging leaven within what is old and settled, and as old and new challenge and answer one another, both move past their former limits. This is also a restatement, in terms of the divine character, of the thesis-antithesis-synthesis principle that ran through the whole study. To share the adventure of growth with each of His children, He makes His spirit dwell within us.
w06.173: That is why Sadler says the true hero of this story is God: the most interesting and fascinating personality in all the wide universe, the author of love and the true wellspring of the adventurous spirit. When He came as one among men, He said, "Follow me," and whoever dares to follow may do so.
w06.174: The Courage and Humility of Speculation
w06.175: Sadler makes no secret that his study has been bold speculation. He draws comfort from two passages. One says that revelation deliberately leaves things unsaid.

w06.176.q: Such conceptual expansion would hardly be desirable as it would deprive the thinking mortals of the next thousand years of that stimulus to creative speculation which these partially revealed concepts supply.

w06.177: The other is the passage he placed on the last line of his book. The human mind sees dimly and understands slowly, and his conjectures surely contain many errors. Yet even at the end a consolation remains.

w06.178.q: All of man's universe romancing may not be fact, but much, very much, is truth.

w06.179: For readers who have followed this commentary, these words also suggest a way of reading. Sadler's reckoning of the ages, his nucleus and cytoplasm, his Third Experiential Trinity, and his ten levels of Deity function are not revealed facts but the speculation of one man who took the revelation as his clue. Even if they should not prove to be fact, the truth they convey, which invites us to read the universe as a story of God's love and adventure, will remain in them for a long time.
w06.180: The epilogue is the counterpart of the prologue. Where the prologue dealt with what existential Deity did before creation, the epilogue imagines what experiential Deity does beyond creation.
w06.181: Sadler resolves the impasse by separating quality from quantity. Absolute destiny can be fully attained in quality even when limited in quantity, and Havona is the prototype.
w06.182: Sadler infers that the Supreme and the Ultimate, joined as the Supreme-Ultimate, trinitize God the Absolute, and that the innermost zone of the Cosmos Infinite appears along with Him. This is analogous, but not homologous, to the Father-Son's trinitizing of the Spirit.
w06.183: With the appearance of God the Absolute the Trinity of Trinities gains its complete second level, which Sadler regards as the "Third Experiential Trinity." Following the text, he takes the third level to be the Universal Absolute.
w06.184: Sadler reads the six partnerships of dual Deity named in The Urantia Book [106:8.12] as "The Processional of Initiative," and he matches the last three partnerships with the three phases of the Cosmos Infinite (inception, realization, consummation).
w06.185: To the seven levels of total Deity, Sadler adds the reassociative, actualizing-potential, and static-dynamic levels, which he sees as mirror images of the first three. All three are Sadler's concepts.
w06.186: The value of God does not change, but His meaning grows. We will find the Father as the Absolute but will forever go on seeking Him as the Infinite.
w06.187: In the Afterword Sadler names God, the source of love and adventure, as the true hero of the whole story, and he hopes that his speculations, even where they are not fact, hold much truth.
w07.001: The Antecedents of the Master Universe
w07.003: In this first appendix Sadler runs a thought experiment backward through time. His point of departure is the eternal core that survives even after outer space and then the superuniverses have emptied out: the Paradise-Havona system. He first takes stock of what the first-age Havona did and did not contain. Then, leaving the domain of fact, he descends through three hypothetical stages that he names the Zero Age, the Pre-Zero concept, and what lies before the Pre-Zero. He closes by showing that the story of origins works just as well when told in reverse, and concludes that the order within eternity is an order of concepts rather than of time.
w07.005: With this chapter the commentary enters its second part and takes up Sadler's appendices one by one. In the twelve chapters of the main text he sketched the broad storyline of the master universe; in the appendices he lifts out the ideas lying underneath that story and examines each in depth. The appendices are therefore more detailed than the chapters, bolder in their reasoning, and much more densely annotated with references to The Urantia Book. The first three deal with the stage itself: what existed before the master universe (Appendix I), what kind of reality the central Isle of Paradise is (Appendix II), and how the space in which the master universe unfolds is organized (Appendix III). Here, as throughout, revealed statements and Sadler's own inferences are kept carefully apart.
w07.006: 1. A Journey Backward in Time (orig. pp. 152–154)
w07.007: Sadler invites us to run the present master universe backward like a reel of film. The further back the reel turns, the fewer stars and nebulae remain in outer space, until outer space stands entirely empty; turn it a little more and the superuniverses grow sparse and finally vanish as well. This is roughly the period The Urantia Book calls the "near-eternity" past or the dawn of time. Yet if we keep rewinding beyond that point, nothing further changes. Paradise is always at the center, and Havona always circles around it. Since nothing at all lay outside it, Havona in that era would not have been the "central" universe but simply "the" universe.

w07.008.q: In brief, the Infinite Spirit testifies that, since he is eternal, so also is the central universe eternal. And this is the traditional starting point of the history of the universe of universes.

w07.009: Sadler sums up the master universe as finding expression three times over: in the perfection of Havona during the first age; in the present age, when the imperfect superuniverses enter into relationship with Havona and together form the grand universe; and in a future in which the still-empty outer universes will be related to the grand universe. The master universe as an idea, however, had been held from the very beginning, as a living blueprint, by the Architects of the Master Universe. The appendix first examines the first age within the realm of fact and then turns to the question of what came "before Havona." Sadler's working premise is that such thinking may yield valid concepts even when it cannot yield facts. The text itself, after all, speaks of a hypothetical moment prior to Havona as the "dawn of eternity."
w07.010: 2. Havona in the First Age (orig. pp. 154–158)
w07.012: The Havona that The Urantia Book describes is in fact the Havona of the second age, our own era. What was it like in the first? Sadler begins by dividing its physical structure into three parts: the three circuits of satellites near Paradise (seven worlds each of the Father, the Son, and the Spirit), the seven planetary circuits carrying the billion spheres, and the two belts of dark gravity bodies at the outer edge. All three, he concludes, already existed in the first age.

w07.013.q: All twenty-one are enormous spheres, and each group of seven is differently eternalized.

w07.014: From the words "differently eternalized" Sadler draws the hint that even within eternity there are gradations of derivation. He also notes that only the seven worlds of the Son share a common physical constitution while the other fourteen each differ, which by his count implies no fewer than fifteen modes of materialization unknown to us. So far as he can tell, the only physical change introduced in the second age was the integration of the central universe's power directors with those of the superuniverses [29:1.3]. What changed dramatically was the activity of personalities.
w07.016: Sadler starts from the text's statement that the Seven Master Spirits are the first personalizations of experiential Deity.

w07.017.q: With the Spirit the existential cycle of Deity personalization attains completion; the primary personalities of the Third Source and Center are experiential and are seven in number.

w07.018: It follows that first-age Havona was a wholly existential universe, containing no beings whose origin came later than that of the Master Spirits. What, then, went on at Ascendington before there were any ascenders? Who dwelt on Sonarington when no descending sons had yet appeared? Divinington may well have been the home of the Father fragments even then, but no Adjuster had yet gone out to indwell a human mind. The text itself says that the membership of these secret spheres is redistributed according to the universe ages [13:2.5].
w07.021: Ascenders on Ascendington, seraphim on Seraphington, Solitary Messengers and power supervisors on Solitarington
w07.022: Executive seats of the Seven Master Spirits; the Seven Supreme Executives
Neither Master Spirits nor Executives, and no superuniverses to co-ordinate
w07.023: Circuit Spirits, power centers, Graduate Guides, Havona Servitals, secondary and tertiary supernaphim
None (only the Havona natives and the eternal beings)
w07.024: Sadler places the appearance of evolutionary growth in Havona well after the start of the second age, probably around the arrival of Grandfanda. That is also when the two-way procession began, with ascenders moving inward and Paradise citizens moving outward. First-age Havona had no outward relationships at all; it faced only inward, toward itself and toward Paradise. Much of what Havona now holds arrived only when it became the nuclear universe of the superuniverses.
w07.025: The inventory of the first age
w07.026: What actually existed in the first age was this: the three persons of Deity, the Paradise Trinity, the three Absolutes of potentiality, the Isle of Paradise with some of its citizens, the Transcendentalers together with the Master Architects who direct them, and Havona with its inhabitants. All of these are eternal and existential, and together they constitute the everlasting core both of total reality and of the master universe. To go further back is to leave the realm of fact behind—though conceptual antecedents can still be explored.
w07.028: In time it is enough to say that a source is older than whatever derives from it. If both are eternal, however, that statement becomes a paradox. Sadler resolves it by borrowing the comparative and superlative forms of the adjective and assigning eternity three "degrees": eternal, more eternal, and most eternal.
w07.029: The Infinite Spirit is eternal, and so is the central universe. The Eternal Son and Paradise are more eternal: the Son is co-ancestor of the Infinite Spirit, and Paradise was already present when Father and Son joined to bring forth the Spirit and Havona. The Universal Father is most eternal, being the Father of the Son and the source of Paradise.

w07.030.q: Nonpersonal and nonspiritual Paradise appears to have been the inevitable repercussion to the Father's will and act which eternalized the Original Son.

w07.031: Sadler pairs these three degrees with the first age, the Zero Age, and the Pre-Zero concept respectively, and then takes one step further to imagine what lies before the Pre-Zero.
w07.032: Four stages in the descent through eternity: what disappears and what remains at each stage (only the first age is fact; the rest are concepts)
w07.034: On entering what Sadler calls the Zero Age we leave the domain of fact but not the domain of valid concept. There is no Infinite Spirit, and therefore neither Havona nor the Trinity. The Father has attained dual expression, in the Son and in Paradise, but not yet triune expression. The Son exists but does not yet function; the Zero Age ends with the Son's first act, the joint deed with the Father from which the Spirit and Havona appear. Paradise likewise exists but is not yet functioning as the source of physical creation. Outside it there is no space, only midspace.
w07.035: The three Absolutes look somewhat different here. The Deity Absolute exists, but since this is before the Trinity and the Father is still diffused throughout Total Deity, Sadler suggests it would be better named the Limited-Absolute.

w07.036.q: With the appearance of coexistent personal Deity, the Eternal Son and the Infinite Spirit, the Father escaped, as a personality, from otherwise inevitable diffusion throughout the potential of Total Deity.

w07.037: The Unqualified Absolute also exists, but in the absence of space it would have had neither a space presence nor any function toward space potency. The Universal Absolute co-ordinates the other two, yet it would not yet have had the task of balancing tensions between absolute and subabsolute reality, since on this view no subabsolute reality existed.
w07.039: But was there really no subabsolute reality? Paradise tradition holds that the three Architects of the Havona level, counseled by the senior Architect, had a share in planning Havona [31:9.4]. Anyone who planned Havona must have existed before it. Sadler adds a bold conjecture. There is a tradition that a 28,012th Architect failed to absonitize, having passed beyond the upper limit of subabsoluteness [31:9.10]. If the senior Architect functions at that "limit of absonity," he might be not the first but the 28,011th, the last possible Architect—in which case the entire company of Architects would have been present in the Zero Age.
w07.040: Sadler offers this as an instance of what might be called the reversibility of sequence: the order in which the Architects appeared is plausible whichever way one counts. A similar paradox touches the Father and the Son. If the Son is the "unqualified spirit personality" that the Father divested Himself of, then in a certain sense the Son comes first. The text says that the citizens of Paradise are conscious of a "⟦Q 11:2.11⟧nontime sequence of events⟦/Q⟧" [11:2.11]. Where there is no time, there can still be order.
w07.041: Sadler and the text: is the senior Architect first or last?
w07.042: The Urantia Book states plainly that the senior Architect is the "⟦Q 31:9.3⟧first-eventuated⟦/Q⟧" [31:9.3]. Reading him as the last of the Architects is a thought experiment of Sadler's that runs against the text, and he himself uses it only to illustrate how a sequence can be read in reverse. It should not be taken as a claim about the actual order of the Architects' eventuation.
w07.043: Did time and space exist? As facts, presumably not. But if the Architects were present, time and space might well have existed as concepts within their absonite minds. Were there Paradise citizens? If the Havona natives are "eternal," the Paradise citizens could be "more eternal." Not all of them, however, since the last of their more than three thousand orders received personality only when the Trinity mandate went forth to organize the superuniverses.
w07.044: 5. The Pre-Zero Concept and Beyond (orig. pp. 161–163)
w07.046: One step further down and the Eternal Son and Paradise vanish too. At this stage, which Sadler calls the Pre-Zero concept, three realities remain. The first is Deity in almost its totality, the Limited-Absolute. Even the name "Universal Father" no longer seems apt here—not because God is absent, but because He is pictured as "pre-Father." God, as absolute personality, is diffused throughout Total Deity. By divesting Himself of this absolute personality He brings the Son into being, and by trinitizing the Spirit together with the Son, the volitional principle of Deity becomes the Universal Father. What remains of Total Deity once the Trinity is subtracted, an infinite residue, is the Deity Absolute of all subsequent ages.
w07.047: The second is the Unqualified Absolute. Deity's free will split all reality into what was deified and what was not, and the whole of the non-Deity side became the Unqualified Absolute. The third is the Universal Absolute, which equalizes the tension created by that division. Sadler repeats more than once that neither the Zero Age nor the Pre-Zero concept is fact; both are valid only as instruments of thought.
w07.048: Before the Pre-Zero: the static moment
w07.049: For the final stage the text itself supplies a remarkable description.

w07.050.q: This is the hypothetical static moment of eternity; actuals are still contained within their potentials, and potentials have not yet appeared within the infinity of the I AM. But even in this conjectured situation we must assume the existence of the possibility of self-will.

w07.051: At this point the deified and the undeified have not yet separated. Sadler nevertheless stresses that The Urantia Book does not accept monism, the doctrine that at the very beginning there was only one kind of reality, because even in this moment there is "the possibility of self-will." The evidence lies in what followed: the potentials did in fact differentiate, and ever since they have been actualized without pause through association, creation, and evolution.
w07.052: Sadler identifies this stage with the first functional level of Total Deity.
w07.054: Here the exploration reaches an unexpected conclusion. The static level is not merely a concept; it is a fact. Total Deity still functions on the static level today, as the text's description of the Universal One of Infinity makes clear [105:2.11]. The eternity of the past is the eternity of the present, and the eternity of the present is the eternity of the future.
w07.055: 6. A Story That Works in Reverse (orig. pp. 163–165)
w07.056: Everything said so far has followed the conventional order the text presents on several occasions: it starts with the Absolutes of potentiality and concludes with the actual Absolutes, namely Paradise, the Son, and the Spirit. Sadler observes that the story can also be told the other way round. In either telling, however, God remains the First Cause.
w07.057: The reversed story starts with the actuals. The Father expresses Himself as the personal and the nonpersonal, that is, as the Son and as Paradise. Son-spirit and Paradise energy lie so close to their source that only their names tell them apart. The Father then co-ordinates the two by mind, whereupon the Infinite Spirit appears, the Trinity becomes a fact, and Havona appears at once [0:12.1]. Only after that do the potentials come on the scene.

w07.058.q: And these undisclosed infinity potentials remain space concealed in the Unqualified Absolute and divinely enshrouded in the Deity Absolute, while these two become one in the functioning of the Universal Absolute, the unrevealed infinity-unity of the Paradise Father.

w07.059: Sadler adds, identifying it as a personal belief, that the Infinite is probably concealed behind the presence and function of the Universal Absolute.
w07.060: Two directions for telling the origin of reality: from potential to actual, and from actual to potential. In both, God is the First Cause
w07.061: If both stories make sense, then the events of eternity have no temporal sequence as matters of fact. There is an "order of concept," but no "order of fact." The text says as much.

w07.062.q: But though we may portray reality origins and infinity differentiation by a sequential narrative, in fact all seven Absolutes are unqualifiedly and co-ordinately eternal.

w07.063: By running time backward as a thought experiment, Sadler arrives at the eternal core that always remains: the Paradise-Havona system.
w07.064: Physically, first-age Havona was much as it is today, but experiential beings such as the Master Spirits, Circuit Spirits, power centers, and Graduate Guides were not yet present.
w07.065: The three degrees of derivation—eternal, more eternal, most eternal—are Sadler's thinking tools, matched to the first age, the Zero Age, and the Pre-Zero concept.
w07.066: Whether the Master Architects existed in the Zero Age remains an open question; treating the senior Architect as the last Architect is a thought experiment at odds with the text.
w07.067: Even in the static moment before the Pre-Zero there is the possibility of self-will, and the static level still functions as a fact today.
w07.068: The story of origins can be told from potential to actual or from actual to potential; eternity knows an order of concepts but not an order of time.
w07.070: Appendix II, Paradise and the Master Universe (pp. 166–176)
w07.071: As the dwelling place of God, Paradise is easy enough to grasp; regarded as one of the Seven Absolutes, it is the most mysterious of them all. Weaving together statements from the text, Sadler shows that Paradise is not part of the master universe but a reality prior to it, the source that bestows space, space potency, and time. He then calculates how many residential units upper Paradise holds, arriving at ten to the power of 2,817, and sets that figure alongside the proportions of the space levels.
w07.073: Among the seven Absolutes of Infinity, Paradise is the one that is both impersonal and non-Deity. Sadler compares it to an "absolute machine" made by God. Just as people build machines to take over repetitive work, God may have done something similar—except that this machine, in some fashion, "knows." What deepens the mystery is its isolation.

w07.074.q: Paradise represents nothing and nothing represents Paradise. It is neither a force nor a presence; it is just Paradise.

w07.075: The three Absolutes of potentiality are unified in the Universal Absolute, and the three persons of Deity are unified in the Trinity. Paradise has no such partner. Sadler regards this isolation as a task God has left for the experiential Deities to resolve, and he returns to it in his discussion of the power-personality synthesis (Appendix XXII).
w07.076: The text joins the Isle and the eternal universe that surrounds it under the name "⟦Q 12:1.11⟧the Paradise-Havona System⟦/Q⟧" [12:1.11]. Neither has an origin in time, but Havona, like the superuniverses, lies within space, while Paradise alone lies outside it. And just as the Son is more eternal than the Spirit, Paradise is "more eternal" than Havona.

w07.077.q: Paradise is the geographic center of infinity; it is not a part of universal creation, not even a real part of the eternal Havona universe.

w07.078: Sadler therefore treats Paradise as a reality "prior to the master universe." In the Zero Age Paradise exists, yet not a fragment of the master universe does. If Havona is the nuclear universe of the superuniverses (Chapter 8), is Paradise then the nucleus of nuclei? He calls the point debatable, yet holds that in one sense Paradise is the true nucleus. The text describes the midspace zones as a relative extension of Paradise [11:7.2], and these zones ultimately enclose all of space. Above all, Paradise is the source of every reality that is neither spirit nor mind. Space, space potency, and time are its bestowals.
w07.079: 2. The Bestowal of Space and Space Potency (orig. pp. 167–170)
w07.080: Sadler gathers the text's statements about space into a table. Paradise does not occupy space. Space is its bestowal and appears to originate just below nether Paradise. Space approaches the absolute without being absolute, is not infinite, and contains and conditions motion.

w07.081.q: Space is not infinite, even though it takes origin from Paradise; not absolute, for it is pervaded by the Unqualified Absolute. We do not know the absolute limits of space, but we do know that the absolute of time is eternity.

w07.082: At this point Sadler reasons as follows. Before Havona there was no space as a fact; beyond Paradise there was only midspace. Space appeared at the "dawn of eternity," at the same moment as the central universe, as if some action of the Isle had pushed outward into midspace.
w07.083: Paradise does not stop at providing space; it also fills that space with something: the entire potential of what will become the matter of every universe, past, present, and future.

w07.084.q: But this cosmic derivation is an eternity event; at no time—past, present, or future—does either space or the material cosmos come forth from the nuclear Isle of Light.

w07.085: Sadler reads "an eternity event" as something that happened once and only once. If so, the bestowal must have been without limit. This potential, charged throughout all space, is space potency, and its stewardship passed to the Unqualified Absolute. To put it in an analogy, Paradise invested an infinite endowment all at once, and the Unqualified Absolute acts as the treasurer who holds it and pays it out as each new universe takes shape. The nature of the Unqualified Absolute is unchanged, but its function begins with the first age. Sadler takes the text's remark that this Absolute is "⟦Q 12:4.2⟧functionally limited to space⟦/Q⟧" [12:4.2] to refer to exactly this function.

w07.086.q: 1. The Deity Absolute seems to be the all-powerful activator, while the Unqualified Absolute appears to be the all-efficient mechanizer of the supremely unified and ultimately co-ordinated universe of universes, even universes upon universes, made, making, and yet to be made.

w07.087: In a phrase that gathers "made, making, and yet to be made" into one, Sadler sees a purely eternal control that disregards time. Mechanizing and activating are two operations that generate tension between them, and resolving that tension is the work of the Universal Absolute. He further surmises that the bestowal of space and space potency may have been Paradise's repercussion to the appearance of the Infinite Spirit, since the God of Action is the activator of Paradise [9:3.8]. He concedes, however, that he cannot say whether the triata of Havona or the dark gravity bodies came directly from Paradise or by way of the Unqualified Absolute.

w07.089.q: Like space, time is a bestowal of Paradise, but not in the same sense, only indirectly. Time comes by virtue of motion and because mind is inherently aware of sequentiality.

w07.090.q: Roughly: space seemingly originates just below nether Paradise; time just above upper Paradise.

w07.091: On Paradise motion is volitional, but outside it everything moves, from the atom to the spheres of Havona. Time is not reckoned on Paradise, though it is reckoned on the Havona circuits, where each of the billion worlds keeps its own local time [14:1.11]. Sadler suggests that sequence may be more fundamental than time. The citizens of Paradise are aware of nontime sequence, and temporal sequence derives from the indirect bestowal of Paradise. Yet, as he himself admits, just "how" the Isle bestows time remains unclear.
w07.093: The text calls Paradise the most gigantic organized body in the master universe [11:0.1] but gives no dimensions. What it does provide are figures for the residential arrangements of the Holy Land on upper Paradise. Of its seven concentric zones, the second belongs to the ascenders from the superuniverses; it is divided into seven sectors, one per superuniverse, and each sector into residential units, each serving a billion working groups.

w07.094.q: One thousand of these units constitute a division. One hundred thousand divisions equal one congregation. Ten million congregations constitute an assembly. One billion assemblies make one grand unit.

w07.095: Residential units up to the first grand unit (number of working groups)
w07.102: Sadler notices that the multipliers run 10³, 10⁵, 10⁷, 10⁹, growing a hundredfold at each step, and he carries this rule all the way through. The grand units continue to the seventh, and then the master, superior, supersuperior, celestial, supercelestial, and supreme units each unfold through seven steps of their own. A single "seventh supreme unit" at the end of the series would contain ten to the power of 2,817 working groups. The arithmetic is easy to check: add every odd number from 3 to 105 to the starting exponent of 9, and the result is 9 + 2,808 = 2,817. Even so, the text says that this arrangement occupies well under one per cent of the area of the second zone.
w07.103: Sadler's count of residential units: over 52 steps the exponent of the number of working groups climbs from 9 to 2,817
w07.104: Sadler and the text: grouping by sevens, multiplying by a hundred
w07.105: The text supplies actual numbers only up to the first grand unit. After that it says only that the grand units continue to the seventh and that the series then expands "by sevens" from the master units to the supreme units. The assumption that each multiplier keeps growing a hundredfold is Sadler's extension of the rule found in the first four steps. Ten to the power of 2,817 is therefore not a revealed number but an estimate meant to convey a sense of scale.
w07.106: Sadler goes on to speculate about the purpose of the seven residential zones. If the first and second zones are for those who originate in the present grand universe, the next four may be intended for those who will one day inhabit the outer space levels, one zone per level, and the seventh for the citizens of the Cosmos Infinite. If the sizes of the zones were proportional to those of the space levels, then by the ratios of Appendix XVI (grand universe 1, primary 100, secondary 10,000, tertiary 1,000,000, quartan 100,000,000), a combined width of one inch for the first two zones would make the sixth zone about 1,600 miles wide. He also points out the weakness of this comparison. Space levels are measured in light-years, but Paradise is not in space, and distance there is a nonspatial "⟦Q 11:2.11⟧absolute distance⟦/Q⟧" [11:2.11]. Still, the laborious calculation makes the text's single line about "the most gigantic organized body" a little more tangible.
w07.107: Paradise is the impersonal, non-Deity Absolute, an isolated reality with no counterpart anywhere in the universes.
w07.108: Havona and Paradise alike have no origin in time, but Havona lies within space and Paradise outside it; Paradise is a reality prior to the master universe.
w07.109: Paradise bestows space, space potency, and time. The bestowal of space potency was a single "eternity event," and its stewardship passed to the Unqualified Absolute.
w07.110: That space appeared together with Havona, as a repercussion to the appearance of the Infinite Spirit, is Sadler's inference.
w07.111: Time is bestowed indirectly, through motion and the mind's awareness of sequence, and sequence itself may be more fundamental than time.
w07.112: The figure of ten to the power of 2,817 residential units is Sadler's estimate, obtained by extending the rule of the text's first four steps.
w07.113: The Space Levels of the Master Universe
w07.114: Appendix III, Space Levels of the Master Universe (pp. 177–189)
w07.115: The master universe is built within the pervaded space that extends horizontally from Paradise, and this space is divided into six space levels. Sadler first argues that space should be regarded as a positive reality, then sets out the boundaries of space, and then walks outward from the edge of Paradise to the far margin of the Quartan Space Level, checking at each stage what the text actually tells us. Finally he speculates on why The Urantia Book makes no mention of the theory of relativity, viewing the question against the history of cosmological models.
w07.116: 1. Two Kinds of Space, and Space as Positive (orig. pp. 177–178)
w07.117: There is unpervaded space, extending above and below Paradise, and pervaded space, extending horizontally; between them lie the midspace zones, which divide them and ultimately enclose both. Since the whole master universe arises within pervaded space, Sadler uses "space" from here on to mean pervaded space only.

w07.118.q: It is a bestowal of Paradise, and the space of the grand universe and that of all outer regions is believed to be actually pervaded by the ancestral space potency of the Unqualified Absolute.

w07.119: We tend to think of space as the place where mass and energy are "not," but The Urantia Book treats space as a positive reality.

w07.120.q: Space is, however, real. It contains and conditions motion. It even moves.

w07.121: Sadler makes the difference vivid by restating a familiar law. Say that "gravity weakens with the square of the distance," and space hides behind the word "distance." Say instead that "space, as a reality, acts upon gravity and diminishes its force in proportion to the square of the distance," and space steps forward as the subject of the sentence. Space is a condition that looks empty yet favors motion and even demands it; its limit lies where midspace, which resists motion, begins.
w07.122: 2. The Six Space Levels and the Boundaries of Space (orig. pp. 178–180)
w07.123: The space of the master universe is divided into the Havona space level, the superuniverse space level, and four outer space levels: the Primary, Secondary, Tertiary, and Quartan Space Levels.

w07.124.q: A space level thus functions as an elliptical region of motion surrounded on all sides by relative motionlessness.

w07.125: Sadler likens a space level to an "elliptical tube" that favors motion, bordered at the sides by zones of relative quiet and above and below by the midspace zones. The direction of rotation alternates from one level to the next.
